claim: Schistosomes are parasitic flatworms infecting hundreds of millions of people.
source: Schistosomes are parasitic flatworms infecting hundreds of millions of people.
evidence: This is a statement about the global health impact of schistosomes, supported by established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Schistosomes alternate between asexual reproduction in molluscan hosts and sexual reproduction in mammalian hosts.
source: These parasites alternate between asexual reproduction in molluscan hosts and sexual reproduction in mammalian hosts; short-lived, water-borne stages infect each host.
evidence: This describes the known life cycle of schistosomes, which is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Schistosomes deploy five body plans throughout their life cycle.
source: Thriving in such disparate environments requires remarkable developmental plasticity, manifested by five body plans deployed throughout the parasite's life cycle.
evidence: This is a factual statement about schistosome morphology based on established knowledge of their life cycle stages.

claim: Subsets of larvally derived stem cells are likely sources of adult stem cells in Schistosoma mansoni.
source: Here, we show that subsets of larvally derived stem cells are likely sources of adult stem cells and the germline.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including single-cell transcriptomics and in situ hybridization.

claim: Subsets of larvally derived stem cells are likely sources of the germline in Schistosoma mansoni.
source: Here, we show that subsets of larvally derived stem cells are likely sources of adult stem cells and the germline.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including gene expression analysis and lineage tracing through developmental stages.

claim: A novel gene serves as the earliest marker for the schistosome germline.
source: We also identify a novel gene that serves as the earliest marker for the schistosome germline, which emerges inside the mammalian host and is ultimately responsible for disease pathology.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing eled expression patterns in developing juveniles.

claim: The schistosome germline emerges inside the mammalian host.
source: We also identify a novel gene that serves as the earliest marker for the schistosome germline, which emerges inside the mammalian host and is ultimately responsible for disease pathology.
evidence: This is supported by data showing eled expression beginning after transformation to schistosomula.

claim: Flatworms include more than 44,000 parasitic species.
source: Flatworms include more than 44,000 parasitic species that form one of the largest groups of metazoan endoparasites (Loker and Hofkin, 2015).
evidence: This is a factual statement supported by a citation to Loker and Hofkin, 2015.

claim: Parasitic flatworms form one of the largest groups of metazoan endoparasites.
source: Flatworms include more than 44,000 parasitic species that form one of the largest groups of metazoan endoparasites (Loker and Hofkin, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Loker and Hofkin, 2015.

claim: Parasitic flatworm life cycles typically involve asexually and sexually reproducing stages.
source: Their life cycles typically involve asexually and sexually reproducing stages, each with its own distinct body plan and strategy to enhance transmission between multiple hosts (Clark, 1974; Pearce and MacDonald, 2002; Viney and Cable, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing parasitic flatworm life cycles.

claim: Each life cycle stage of parasitic flatworms has its own distinct body plan.
source: Their life cycles typically involve asexually and sexually reproducing stages, each with its own distinct body plan and strategy to enhance transmission between multiple hosts (Clark, 1974; Pearce and MacDonald, 2002; Viney and Cable, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on parasitic flatworm biology.

claim: Schistosoma infects over 250 million people.
source: Focusing on the cells that may drive such parasitic life cycles, we study Schistosoma, a parasitic flatworm infecting over 250 million people, which causes the major neglected tropical disease, schistosomiasis (Hoffmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a factual statement about disease burden supported by citation to Hoffmann et al., 2014.

claim: Schistosoma causes schistosomiasis, a major neglected tropical disease.
source: Focusing on the cells that may drive such parasitic life cycles, we study Schistosoma, a parasitic flatworm infecting over 250 million people, which causes the major neglected tropical disease, schistosomiasis (Hoffmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Each miracidium carries 10–20 germinal cells.
source: Each miracidium carries 10–20 germinal cells (Pan, 1980; Cort et al., 1954; Wang et al., 2013), which expand massively and differentiate to produce many daughter sporocysts (Figure 1A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by the authors' own work.

claim: Germinal cells expand massively and differentiate to produce many daughter sporocysts.
source: Each miracidium carries 10–20 germinal cells (Pan, 1980; Cort et al., 1954; Wang et al., 2013), which expand massively and differentiate to produce many daughter sporocysts (Figure 1A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations and visual evidence in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Germinal cells exhibit heterogeneity within the population.
source: Our recent work has shown that germinal cells exhibit heterogeneity within this population (Wang et al., 2013), revealed by the distinct proliferation kinetics and expression of a schistosome homolog of nanos (Wang and Lehmann, 1991), a conserved regulator of germ cell development (Juliano et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2007) also expressed in the schistosome adult stem cells (Collins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work and other studies.

claim: Principal component analysis of single-cell transcriptomes revealed three major cell classes in sporocyst stem cells.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of single-cell transcriptomes revealed three major cell classes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The three sporocyst stem cell classes are designated κ-cells (klf+nanos-2+), φ-cells (fgfrA,B+), and δ-cells (nanos-2+fgfrA,B+).
source: We designated these classes based upon their respective markers: κ-cells (kappa indicates klf+nanos-2+); φ-cells (phi indicates fgfrA,B+); and δ-cells (delta indicates double-positive for nanos-2 and fgfrA,B).
evidence: This is based on single-cell transcriptomic data and validated by FISH.

claim: The difference between κ and δ/φ-cells extends along PC1 and contributes to ~30% of the total variance among cells.
source: The difference between κ and δ/φ-cells extends along PC1, and contributes to ~30% of the total variance among cells, whereas the difference between δ and φ-cells is secondary, delineated by PC2 and contributing ~10% of the total variance.
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis of single-cell transcriptomic data.

claim: The difference between δ and φ-cells is delineated by PC2 and contributes ~10% of the total variance.
source: The difference between κ and δ/φ-cells extends along PC1, and contributes to ~30% of the total variance among cells, whereas the difference between δ and φ-cells is secondary, delineated by PC2 and contributing ~10% of the total variance.
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis of single-cell transcriptomic data.

claim: A schistosome p53 homolog is expressed abundantly in δ-cells and at lower levels in φ-cells.
source: Based on projections along the first two PCs (Treutlein et al., 2014), we identified additional genes that contribute to the distinctions between classes: a schistosome p53 homolog and a zinc finger protein (zfp-1) expressed abundantly in δ-cells and at lower levels in φ-cells; and a hes family transcription factor (hesl) expressed specifically in φ-cells (Figure 1D and E, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: A zinc finger protein (zfp-1) is expressed abundantly in δ-cells and at lower levels in φ-cells.
source: Based on projections along the first two PCs (Treutlein et al., 2014), we identified additional genes that contribute to the distinctions between classes: a schistosome p53 homolog and a zinc finger protein (zfp-1) expressed abundantly in δ-cells and at lower levels in φ-cells; and a hes family transcription factor (hesl) expressed specifically in φ-cells (Figure 1D and E, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: A hes family transcription factor (hesl) is expressed specifically in φ-cells.
source: Based on projections along the first two PCs (Treutlein et al., 2014), we identified additional genes that contribute to the distinctions between classes: a schistosome p53 homolog and a zinc finger protein (zfp-1) expressed abundantly in δ-cells and at lower levels in φ-cells; and a hes family transcription factor (hesl) expressed specifically in φ-cells (Figure 1D and E, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The transcriptomic findings were validated by fluorescent in situ hybridization on in vitro-cultured mother sporocysts.
source: We validated these transcriptomic findings by fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) on in vitro-cultured mother sporocysts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: klf was expressed at very low levels, beneath the detection limits of the FISH protocol.
source: Unfortunately, the κ class-specific marker klf was expressed at very low levels (Figure 1E), beneath the detection limits of our current FISH protocol.
evidence: This is based on expression data shown in Figure 1E and technical limitations of FISH.

claim: φ-cells were distributed beneath the parasite's outer layer and excluded from daughter embryos.
source: φ-cells were distributed beneath the parasite's outer layer and excluded from daughter embryos.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data showing spatial distribution of cell types.

claim: δ-cells were found in large clusters within embryos.
source: δ-cells were found in large clusters within embryos.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data showing spatial distribution of cell types.

claim: κ-cells clustered with δ-cells in embryos and were found in extraembryonic tissues as singlets or doublets.
source: κ-cells clustered with δ-cells in embryos and were found in extraembryonic tissues as singlets or doublets, suggested to be the source of developing embryos in previous histological studies (Schutte, 1974).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data and supported by citation to previous histological work.

claim: κ-cells comprised the vast majority (>85%) of stem cells in mature daughter sporocysts two weeks post-infection.
source: Two weeks post-infection, mother sporocysts contain many mature daughter sporocysts that are ready to leave the mother and migrate elsewhere in the snail. At this stage κ-cells comprised the vast majority (>85%) of stem cells in these daughters (Figure 2B); fewer δ-cells were observed and φ-cells were mostly excluded.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of FISH data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All three cell classes reappeared as intermingled populations one week after daughter sporocysts colonized new regions of host tissue.
source: However, one week later, when post-migratory daughters colonized new regions of host tissue (Figure 2C), all three classes reappeared as intermingled populations, consistent with κ-cells generating the other stem cell types.
evidence: This is based on FISH data shown in Figure 2C and supports an inference about cell lineage relationships.

claim: κ-cells generate the other stem cell types.
source: However, one week later, when post-migratory daughters colonized new regions of host tissue (Figure 2C), all three classes reappeared as intermingled populations, consistent with κ-cells generating the other stem cell types.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that κ-cells dominate in pre-migratory daughters and all three classes reappear after migration.

claim: In early cercarial embryos, φ-cells were found concentrated both anteriorly and posteriorly, where the mouth and tail bud form.
source: In early cercarial embryos (dashed circle in Figure 2D–2E), φ-cells were found concentrated both anteriorly and posteriorly, where the mouth and tail bud form, respectively.
evidence: This is based on FISH data shown in Figure 2D-2E.

claim: Two clusters of κ-cells were observed posterior to the penetration glands in early cercarial embryos.
source: Additionally, two clusters of κ-cells were observed posterior to the penetration glands (Figure 2D–2E), at the site of the germinal cell cluster, considered gonadal primordia based on histological and ultrastructural studies (Cheng and Bier, 1972; Dorsey et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on FISH data shown in Figure 2D-2E and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the mature cercarial body, the κ-cell pair posterior to the glands expands into two clusters that contain multiple cells each.
source: In the mature cercarial body (Figure 2F–2G), the κ-cell pair posterior to the glands expands into two clusters that contain multiple cells each.
evidence: This is based on FISH data shown in Figure 2F-2G.

claim: Five δ-cells were detected in a regular pattern around the penetration glands in mature cercarial bodies.
source: In parallel, five δ-cells were detected in a regular pattern around the penetration glands, with one at the midline and two pairs laterally (Figure 2E), whereas φ-cells are absent at this stage.
evidence: This is based on FISH data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: φ-cells are absent in mature cercarial bodies.
source: In parallel, five δ-cells were detected in a regular pattern around the penetration glands, with one at the midline and two pairs laterally (Figure 2E), whereas φ-cells are absent at this stage.
evidence: This is based on FISH data showing no φ-cell markers in mature cercariae.

claim: Only δ and κ-cells, but not φ-cells, may be passed to the intramammalian (sexual) stage.
source: Since the cercarial body (but not the tail) penetrates the mammalian host, only δ and κ-cells, but not φ-cells, may be passed to the intramammalian (sexual) stage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that φ-cells are absent from cercarial bodies and only bodies penetrate the host.

claim: Between 22 and 36 hr post-transformation, five EdU+ cells were observed around the penetration glands, anterior to the ventral sucker.
source: Between 22 and 36 hr post-transformation, we observed five EdU+ cells around the penetration glands, anterior to the ventral sucker (Figure 3B), and confirmed that they were δ-cells (fgfrA+nanos-2+) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on EdU labeling and FISH data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The five EdU+ cells observed 22-36 hr post-transformation were confirmed to be δ-cells (fgfrA+nanos-2+).
source: Between 22 and 36 hr post-transformation, we observed five EdU+ cells around the penetration glands, anterior to the ventral sucker (Figure 3B), and confirmed that they were δ-cells (fgfrA+nanos-2+) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on EdU labeling combined with FISH for fgfrA and nanos-2 shown in Figure 3C.

claim: During the 12 hr after initial EdU labeling, the five δ-cells completed mitosis, indicated by the appearance of five EdU+ doublets.
source: During the next 12 hr, these cells completed mitosis, indicated by the appearance of five EdU+ doublets (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on EdU labeling data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: One week after transformation, two clusters of ~2–3 EdU+ cells appeared in the 'germinal cell cluster' region posterior to the ventral sucker, where κ-cells are found.
source: Thereafter, the number of EdU+ nuclei steadily increased (Figure 3D), but proliferation was restricted anteriorly to the ventral sucker, until one week later, when two clusters of ~2–3 EdU+ cells appeared in the 'germinal cell cluster' region posterior to the ventral sucker, where κ-cells are found (Figure 3B, Days 9–10).
evidence: This is based on EdU labeling data shown in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: EdU+ cells were not detected in irradiated worms.
source: EdU+ cells were not detected in irradiated worms (Figure 3E), consistent with previous reports that irradiation leads to developmental defects and reduced pathogenicity (Wilson, 2009).
evidence: This is based on EdU labeling data shown in Figure 3E and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A small, fixed number of κ and δ-cells are transmitted to the mammalian host.
source: These results suggest that a small, fixed number of κ and δ-cells are transmitted to the mammalian host.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of specific numbers of proliferating cells at defined locations after transformation.

claim: κ and δ-cells are likely the source of the stem cells in adult schistosomes.
source: Because these cells appear to be the only dividing cells in schistosomula, they are likely the source of the recently identified stem cells in adult schistosomes (Collins et al., 2013; 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on EdU labeling data and supported by citations to previous work identifying adult stem cells.

claim: EdU labeling revealed a posterior growth zone (PGZ) that extended as the parasites grew.
source: EdU labeling revealed a posterior growth zone (PGZ) that extended as the parasites grew (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on EdU labeling data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In more mature juveniles, all cells in primordial testes and ovaries incorporated EdU.
source: In more mature juveniles, all cells in primordial testes and ovaries also incorporated EdU (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on EdU labeling data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Five-hundred and seventy-three genes were commonly enriched in both juvenile and sporocyst proliferating cell populations.
source: Five-hundred and seventy-three genes were commonly enriched in both populations, including previously identified schistosome stem cell markers (e.g. nanos-2, ago2-1, and fgfrA), and cell cycle-associated transcripts (h2a, cyclin B, and PCNA) (Wang et al., 2013; Collins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on transcriptomic comparison between juvenile and sporocyst stem cells.

claim: Proliferating cells from juveniles resemble sporocyst stem cells both morphologically and transcriptionally.
source: Taken together, proliferating cells from juveniles resemble the sporocyst stem cells both morphologically and transcriptionally (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that these cells represent juvenile stem cells, which support both somatic growth and germline development in the mammalian host.
evidence: This is based on morphological observations and transcriptomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of 85 juvenile stem cells distinguishes two major cell classes.
source: Hierarchical clustering identified two major cell classes (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on single-cell qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: δ'-cells are similar to δ-cells, but express abundantly both δ and φ-cell markers.
source: δ'-cells are similar to δ-cells, but express abundantly both δ and φ-cell markers (including nanos-2, fgfrA, p53, zfp-1, and hesl), indicating that these cells are the likely source of the adult somatic stem cells (Collins et al., 2013; 2016).
evidence: This is based on single-cell qPCR data and supported by citations to previous work on adult stem cells.

claim: δ'-cells are the likely source of the adult somatic stem cells.
source: δ'-cells are similar to δ-cells, but express abundantly both δ and φ-cell markers (including nanos-2, fgfrA, p53, zfp-1, and hesl), indicating that these cells are the likely source of the adult somatic stem cells (Collins et al., 2013; 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression patterns and supported by citations.

claim: eled is undetectable in sporocysts but is among the most abundant transcripts in juvenile stem cells.
source: The other class abundantly expresses a novel schistosome-specific factor, eledh (eled), which is undetectable in sporocysts but is among the most abundant transcripts in juvenile stem cells (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on single-cell qPCR and RNAseq data comparing sporocyst and juvenile stem cells.

claim: ε-cells display lower expression of nanos-2 and fgfrA, and similar to κ-cells, lack expression of p53, zfp-1, and hesl.
source: We designated this class ε (epsilon indicates eled+), which displays lower expression of nanos-2 and fgfrA, and similar to κ-cells, lacks expression of p53, zfp-1, and hesl (Figure 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on single-cell qPCR data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: ε-cells are likely derivatives of κ-cells.
source: Based on these similarities in gene expression, we propose that ε-cells are likely derivatives of κ-cells (see Discussion for more details).
evidence: This is an inference based on similarities in gene expression patterns between ε-cells and κ-cells.

claim: eled is a single-copy gene (Smp_041540).
source: eled is a single-copy gene (Smp_041540) that was previously annotated as a nuclear hormone receptor, dhr4 (Protasio et al., 2012; Berriman et al., 2009); however, our analysis suggests that this gene does not encode a hormone receptor (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and supported by citations to genome annotations.

claim: eled was previously annotated as a nuclear hormone receptor, dhr4, but does not encode a hormone receptor.
source: eled is a single-copy gene (Smp_041540) that was previously annotated as a nuclear hormone receptor, dhr4 (Protasio et al., 2012; Berriman et al., 2009); however, our analysis suggests that this gene does not encode a hormone receptor (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and contradicts previous annotations.

claim: Homologs of eled are found across Schistosoma species.
source: Homologs of eled are found across Schistosoma species, whereas planarian and tapeworm genomes appear to lack them.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis across flatworm species.

claim: Planarian and tapeworm genomes appear to lack eled homologs.
source: Homologs of eled are found across Schistosoma species, whereas planarian and tapeworm genomes appear to lack them.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis across flatworm species.

claim: eled has a transmembrane domain at the N-terminus with ~100% probability.
source: Figure 4D shows the predicted architecture of eled, which has a transmembrane domain at the N-terminus (probability ~100%), a putative transmembrane domain at the C-terminus (probability ~35%), and an extracellular domain in between (probability ~85%).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction of protein structure shown in Figure 4D.

claim: eled has a putative transmembrane domain at the C-terminus with ~35% probability.
source: Figure 4D shows the predicted architecture of eled, which has a transmembrane domain at the N-terminus (probability ~100%), a putative transmembrane domain at the C-terminus (probability ~35%), and an extracellular domain in between (probability ~85%).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction of protein structure shown in Figure 4D.

claim: eled has an extracellular domain with ~85% probability.
source: Figure 4D shows the predicted architecture of eled, which has a transmembrane domain at the N-terminus (probability ~100%), a putative transmembrane domain at the C-terminus (probability ~35%), and an extracellular domain in between (probability ~85%).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction of protein structure shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The extracellular domain of eled contains 19% serine and 17% threonine, presenting the highest serine/threonine fraction in known proteins.
source: The extracellular domain contains 19% serine and 17% threonine, presenting the highest serine/threonine fraction in known proteins.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of the eled protein.

claim: In juveniles, eled expression was detected in primordial testes, ovaries, and vitellaria, as well as in a gradient increasing toward the PGZ.
source: In juveniles eled expression was detected in primordial testes, ovaries, and vitellaria, as well as in a gradient increasing toward the PGZ, which lacks reproductive organs in males (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on FISH data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: All gonadal eled+ cells are also h2a+.
source: Quantitatively, overlay of eled and h2a revealed that all gonadal eled+ cells (Figure 5B) and ~80% of somatic eled+ cells (966/1269, from two male juveniles) were also h2a+.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of double FISH data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ~80% of somatic eled+ cells are also h2a+.
source: Quantitatively, overlay of eled and h2a revealed that all gonadal eled+ cells (Figure 5B) and ~80% of somatic eled+ cells (966/1269, from two male juveniles) were also h2a+.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of double FISH data from two male juveniles.

claim: All germ cells within gonadal primordia are eled+.
source: Conversely, all germ cells within gonadal primordia were eled+, but only ~50% of the somatic h2a+ cells in the PGZ (1679/3576) and ~10% of the somatic h2a+ cells outside the PGZ (769/5366) expressed eled.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of double FISH data.

claim: ~50% of the somatic h2a+ cells in the PGZ express eled.
source: Conversely, all germ cells within gonadal primordia were eled+, but only ~50% of the somatic h2a+ cells in the PGZ (1679/3576) and ~10% of the somatic h2a+ cells outside the PGZ (769/5366) expressed eled.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of double FISH data.

claim: ~10% of the somatic h2a+ cells outside the PGZ express eled.
source: Conversely, all germ cells within gonadal primordia were eled+, but only ~50% of the somatic h2a+ cells in the PGZ (1679/3576) and ~10% of the somatic h2a+ cells outside the PGZ (769/5366) expressed eled.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of double FISH data.

claim: In mature adults, eled expression was limited to reproductive organs.
source: In mature adults, eled expression was limited to reproductive organs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on FISH data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Somatic ε-cells may be a transitory source of new tissue underlying massive juvenile growth in the PGZ.
source: Thus, somatic ε-cells may be a transitory source of new tissue underlying massive juvenile growth in the PGZ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that eled is expressed in the PGZ in juveniles but not in adults.

claim: eled expression precedes nanos-1 expression in gonadal primordia.
source: We found that eled expression precedes nanos-1, which is germline specific both in juveniles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and adults (Iyer et al., 2016; Wang and Collins, 2016): only a subset of eled+ cells in gonadal primordia co-express nanos-1, and the number of eled+nanos-1+ cells increases over the course of development (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is based on double FISH data shown in Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and supported by citations.

claim: nanos-1 is germline specific in juveniles and adults.
source: We found that eled expression precedes nanos-1, which is germline specific both in juveniles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and adults (Iyer et al., 2016; Wang and Collins, 2016): only a subset of eled+ cells in gonadal primordia co-express nanos-1, and the number of eled+nanos-1+ cells increases over the course of development (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is based on FISH data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations.

claim: The number of eled+nanos-1+ cells increases over the course of development.
source: We found that eled expression precedes nanos-1, which is germline specific both in juveniles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and adults (Iyer et al., 2016; Wang and Collins, 2016): only a subset of eled+ cells in gonadal primordia co-express nanos-1, and the number of eled+nanos-1+ cells increases over the course of development (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is based on double FISH data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: There is a sharp transition at worm length ~400 µm: before the transition, none of the gonadal eled+ cells is nanos-1+; after the transition, most if not all of the gonadal eled+ cells become nanos-1+.
source: Quantification reveals a sharp transition as worm length exceeds ~400 µm: before the transition, none of the gonadal eled+ cells is nanos-1+; after the transition, most if not all of the gonadal eled+ cells become nanos-1+ (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of double FISH data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Germ cells may be derived from ε-cells early in juvenile development.
source: These results suggest that germ cells may be derived from ε-cells early in juvenile development, and eled is the earliest germline marker yet identified in schistosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that eled expression precedes nanos-1 in gonadal primordia.

claim: eled is the earliest germline marker yet identified in schistosomes.
source: These results suggest that germ cells may be derived from ε-cells early in juvenile development, and eled is the earliest germline marker yet identified in schistosomes.
evidence: This is based on the observation that eled is expressed before nanos-1 in developing germ cells.

claim: eled RNAi resulted in upregulation of nanos-2 in the PGZ.
source: eled RNAi resulted in upregulation of nanos-2 in the PGZ (Figure 7A), where the somatic ε- cells are located.
evidence: This is based on WISH data after RNAi shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Knockdown of nanos-1 or nanos-2 resulted in degenerated testes and loss of differentiated germ cells.
source: Knockdown of nanos-1 or nanos-2 resulted in degenerated testes and loss of differentiated germ cells; however, the remaining gonads maintained eled expression (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is based on WISH and confocal microscopy data after RNAi shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: After nanos-1 or nanos-2 knockdown, the remaining gonads maintained eled expression.
source: Knockdown of nanos-1 or nanos-2 resulted in degenerated testes and loss of differentiated germ cells; however, the remaining gonads maintained eled expression (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is based on WISH data after RNAi shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Knockdown of eled resulted in premature accumulation of sperm in juvenile testes.
source: By contrast, knockdown of eled resulted in premature accumulation of sperm in juvenile testes (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data after RNAi shown in Figure 7B.

claim: eled appears to inhibit germ cell differentiation.
source: Thus, eled appears to inhibit, whereas nanos genes are required for, germ cell differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that eled knockdown leads to premature sperm accumulation.

claim: nanos genes are required for germ cell differentiation.
source: Thus, eled appears to inhibit, whereas nanos genes are required for, germ cell differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that nanos knockdown leads to loss of differentiated germ cells.

claim: eled antagonizes the two schistosome nanos homologs: in the soma, it suppresses nanos-2 expression in ε-cells in the PGZ; in the germline, it inhibits germ cell differentiation.
source: Together, these results suggest that eled antagonizes the two schistosome nanos homologs: in the soma, it suppresses nanos-2 expression in ε-cells in the PGZ; in the germline, it inhibits germ cell differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNAi experiments showing opposite effects of eled and nanos knockdown.

claim: κ-cells serve as 'embryonic' stem cells.
source: We posit that κ cells serve as 'embryonic' stem cells: in addition to nanos-2 they express a klf homolog and are found isolated in developing mother sporocysts.
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression patterns and spatial distribution of κ-cells.

claim: Scattered stem cells may persist in mother sporocysts for months and continuously undergo asymmetric divisions.
source: These studies reported that the scattered stem cells may persist in mother sporocysts for months and continuously undergo asymmetric divisions, with one daughter cell forming an embryo while the other remains undifferentiated (Schutte, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schutte, 1974.

claim: κ-cells generate the other stem cell types observed in post-migratory daughter sporocysts.
source: We found that κ-cells are dramatically enriched in mature, pre-migratory daughter sporocysts, consistent with the idea that these cells generate the other stem cell types observed in post-migratory daughter sporocysts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that κ-cells dominate in pre-migratory daughters and all cell types reappear after migration.

claim: δ-cells serve to generate somatic tissues.
source: Activation of several genes associated with somatic stem cell function in adults (e.g. fgfrA/B; p53; zfp-1) leads to the specification of δ-cells from κ-cells; we propose that δ-cells serve to generate somatic tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression patterns and the observation that these genes are associated with somatic stem cell function.

claim: Downregulation of nanos-2 and activation of hesl in δ-cells leads to the formation of φ-cells.
source: We suggest that downregulation of nanos-2 and activation of hesl in δ-cells leads to the formation of φ-cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression patterns distinguishing φ-cells from δ-cells.

claim: φ-cells appear to be a lineage-committed, transit-amplifying population that produces temporary larval tissues.
source: Our previous work identified rapidly cycling stem cells that do not express nanos-2 (in contrast to slower-cycling cells that do) (Wang et al., 2013); thus, φ-cells appear to be a lineage-committed, transit-amplifying population that produces temporary larval tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression patterns, proliferation kinetics, and spatial distribution of φ-cells, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: δ-cells serve as the source of the somatic stem cells identified in adult schistosomes.
source: Given the similarities between the transcriptional profiles of δ-cells and the somatic stem cells found in juvenile parasites (δ'-cells that also express hesl), as well as their early proliferation upon penetrating host skin, we suggest that δ-cells serve as the source of the somatic stem cells identified in adult schistosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on transcriptional similarities and proliferation patterns.

claim: κ-cells downregulate nanos-2 and activate expression of eled to form ε-cells.
source: Based on the antagonistic interaction between eled and nanos, we suggest that κ-cells downregulate nanos-2 and activate expression of eled.
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression patterns and functional interactions between eled and nanos.

claim: The absence of δ/δ'-cell markers in both κ and ε-cells favors the model that κ/ε-cells form a separate lineage from δ/δ'-cells.
source: The absence of δ/δ'-cell markers, fgfr, zfp-1, p53, and hesl, in both κ and ε-cells favors the model that κ/ε-cells form a separate lineage from δ/δ'-cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression patterns distinguishing these cell populations.

claim: ε-cells can either give rise to germline or to a transient somatic population that appears to drive the massive posterior growth exhibited by these parasites.
source: Thus, ε-cells can either give rise to germline or to a transient somatic population that appears to drive the massive posterior growth exhibited by these parasites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that eled is expressed in both gonadal primordia and the PGZ.

claim: The activation of nanos-1 commits ε-cells to germline fate.
source: During maturation, gonadal ε-cells subsequently activate germline-specific nanos-1. We suggest that the activation of nanos-1 commits ε-cells to germline fate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that nanos-1 is germline-specific and its expression follows eled expression.

claim: Under experimental conditions, eled (RNAi) males exhibited premature production of sperm.
source: Under these experimental conditions, eled (RNAi) males exhibited premature production of sperm; thus, eled appears to act as a brake on germ cell differentiation.
evidence: This is based on RNAi experiments and confocal microscopy observations.

claim: The heterogeneity detected in schistosome stem cells is reminiscent of that observed in the planarian neoblasts.
source: The heterogeneity we detected in schistosome stem cells is also reminiscent of that observed in the planarian neoblasts (van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014), and we observed a striking overlap in a group of genes co-regulated between stem cell classes from both organisms.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data on planarian neoblasts, supported by citation.

claim: The genes fgfr, zfp-1, and p53 were defined as markers of an epidermally committed population in planarians.
source: The genes fgfr, zfp-1, and p53 were defined as markers of an epidermally committed population in planarians (van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014.

claim: Schistosome adult stem cells have a strong differentiation bias toward the tegumental lineage.
source: Recently, schistosome adult stem cells were shown to have a strong differentiation bias toward the tegumental lineage (Collins et al., 2016); the necessity of zfp-1 family genes for proper tegumental fate or, more generally, for proper differentiation, further linked these parasites to their free-living ancestors (Wendt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Collins et al., 2016 and Wendt et al., 2018.

claim: In the planarian embryo, blastomeres produce temporary embryonic tissues but also give rise to neoblasts by downregulating a set of embryo-specific genes and upregulating genes associated with adult development (e.g., zfp-1 and p53).
source: Furthermore, in the planarian embryo, blastomeres produce temporary embryonic tissues but also give rise to neoblasts by downregulating a set of embryo-specific genes and upregulating genes associated with adult development (e.g., zfp-1 and p53) (Davies et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Davies et al., 2017.

claim: A similar transition to that observed in planarian embryos may occur between κ-cells and δ/δ'-cells in schistosomes.
source: Our data suggest that a similar transition may also occur between κ-cells and δ/δ'-cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on similarities in gene expression patterns between schistosome and planarian stem cell transitions.

claim: Schistosome infection is currently treated with a single drug, praziquantel.
source: Schistosome infection is currently treated with a single drug, praziquantel, which is used in mass drug administration programs (Hoffmann et al., 2014; Sokolow et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: There are concerns about resistant strains of schistosomes emerging.
source: With concerns about resistant strains emerging (Hoffmann et al., 2014), it becomes increasingly important to understand the fundamental mechanisms driving the propagation and long-term survival of these parasites.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hoffmann et al., 2014.
